en: *The Collection of the Rākṣasa of Ignorance*, Scroll One (alternatively in one scroll or two scrolls).
Now, these three scrolls—whose translator’s name is lost and which are appended to the Qin Records—concern the twelve links of dependent origination.
These are the root of birth and death, the dwelling place and lair of all sentient beings. Heaven... [text ends]
Within the realm where Māra Pāpīyān dwells,

if there are those with wisdom who can contemplate the various faults and afflictions of causes and conditions, thereby forever severing birth and death and transcending the realm of Māra, then at that time the celestial Māras will give rise to great sorrow and distress.

The great ocean of causes and conditions is deep, vast, and boundless; when a wise person enters into it, they are like a caravan leader who, having observed its nature and characteristics and attained full understanding, immediately obtains the supreme treasure of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is the most excellent and most wondrous among all mantras.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have cultivated the six pāramitās, accumulated all virtuous deeds, and severed all fetters and afflictions. Having made firm vows against the māra of the aggregates, the māra of death, and the māra of afflictions, they have forever severed birth and death, transcended the triple world, accomplished the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, attained unimpeded wisdom regarding all dharmas, and act as great luminous witnesses for all sentient beings.

Those who have realized nirvana are true and virtuous friends to the sentient beings of the three realms; they are able to turn the wheel of Dharma, blow the great Dharma conch, beat the great Dharma drum, light the great Dharma lamp, construct the great Dharma bridge, launch the great Dharma ship, and raise the great Dharma sail, proclaiming in a loud voice:

"To those who would cross to the other shore, may their great vows be fully perfected; may all followers of external paths be subdued and defeated; may all those with whom there is a karmic affinity be delivered and liberated; and may all humans and devas give rise to faith and understanding."

Thus, regarding all other phenomena, this Great Being does not give rise to the thought that they are unprecedented; rather, toward the law of dependent origination, he conceives a sense of profound rarity:
"Only the Buddha-Tathāgata is able to exhaustively understand this profound meaning; it cannot be comprehended by any other wise person."

Even such figures as the Great Seer (Maharṣi) and Hāritī, who relied on their own wisdom to give rise to great arrogance, were still obscured by the cataracts of ignorance; though they composed various sūtras and śāstras through tainted knowledge, they could not escape the delusions of false views.

Furthermore, though they wore grass garments, practiced fasting, dwelt in solitary seclusion, and performed hundreds of thousands of ascetic austerities, they ultimately could not attain even a slight liberation from within the cycle of birth and death.
All sentient beings, shrouded by ignorance, give rise to craving.

Due to the conditions of craving, they enter the great ocean where they are overturned by fierce winds; they traverse vast wildernesses and perilous precipices; they are placed upon the battlefield of death to slaughter one another, undergoing all manner of immeasurable suffering and affliction.

If one can deeply understand the twelve links of dependent origination, one will see that within these three realms and five destinies, various karmic actions are performed and diverse forms are received through these causes and conditions.

It is like a skilled musician of the world who can cause the eight musical tones—gong, shang, and the rest—to be harmonious, with their pitches and rhythms corresponding as they are performed together;
or like a master painter, who skillfully applies various colors to produce distinct forms and diverse images that appear vividly and distinctly.
The twelve links of dependent origination are likewise thus: they skillfully harmonize to produce the fruits of karma, causing the cycle of birth and death to revolve without end.
It is like the *kiṃnara* insect, which undergoes three stages of transformation: first it becomes the color of earth, then it becomes red, and finally it becomes black.

The twelve links of dependent origination are likewise thus: they can transform sentient beings into old age, sickness, and death; into the three realms of existence, the five destinies, the four great poisonous snakes, the evil thieves of the five aggregates, and the empty village of the six sense bases.
They can also transform them into universal monarchs, Śakra, Brahmā, the four heavenly kings, and minor kings who enjoy all manner of pleasures;

or into human bodies of noble or humble status, rich or poor, wise or foolish, long-lived or short-lived; or into the forms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, undergoing unspeakable numbers of bitter sufferings.
In this world, the World-Honored One, awakened alone without a teacher, used the surgical probe of wisdom to extract the cataracts of ignorance from the eyes of Kauṇḍinya and others;
with the great rain of Dharma, he extinguished the blazing fires of affliction in Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and others;
and with the supreme medicinal drug of wisdom arising from the conditions of knowledge, he cured the diseases of the fetters in Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others.
With this hook of wisdom, he drew Mahākāśyapa into the Buddha’s true path;
with the ladder of the Dharma, he led the Brahmin Mahāsthala toward the hall of liberation;

and with this axe of wisdom, he felled the trees of the body-attachment of the venerable Mahākātyāyana, Aniruddha, the great Pūrṇa, Mahākauṣṭhila, Nanda, and Sundarananda, as well as other such Arhats.
By means of this true wisdom, he was able to eliminate the Brahma King’s conception that he possessed all-encompassing knowledge;
by the power of this wisdom, he was able to cause the Lord of Devas to seek to become his disciple;
and by means of this wealth of Dharma, he shared it with King Bimbisāra and his retinue of eighty-four thousand people, satisfying them all without any depletion.
By means of this correct wisdom, he caused King Śuklodana to become a Dharma Prince;
by means of this great wisdom, he rescued the most wicked Aṅgulimāla from the suffering of the Avīci hell;
and he was able to turn Brahmins and householders toward the Right Path.
They are able to perform such great acts of adornment as to cause women of shallow wisdom to enter into profound awakening.
By such power, they are able to subdue the Brahmin Dīrghanakha and destroy the fierce strength of Satyaka Nirgrantha;
they can cause the Brahmin Ambaṣṭha to give rise to great terror.
It can quell the notion of great wisdom in the Śīlaprabha Brahmin.
By means of this nectar, even those who are infantile and foolish, upon drinking it, shall all become possessed of great wisdom;
by the power of this mantra, one cannot be stung by the four great venomous snakes, nor can the thieves with drawn swords of the [five] aggregates pursue one.
By means of this Dharma-eye, one perceives the six sense bases as an empty village;
by means of this Dharma-army, one destroys the enemies of the five hindrances; being able to protect the head of wisdom, one does not fear the five desires;
and by means of this vessel of wisdom, one crosses the great ocean of the waves of fetters to reach the shore of Nirvana.
By means of this wisdom, one crosses the great river of ashes, so that neither the internal nor external sense bases (*āyatana*) are scorched or boiled.
It enables one such that the thorns of painful sensations may prick but do not enter;
it enables one not to become lost or submerged within the great darkness of ignorance.

If there are sentient beings who are able to observe, [the Dharma] acts as a lamp for them; it establishes sentient beings upon the level ground of ethical discipline (*śīla*), provides the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as a place of rest, leads them onto the path of right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) to enter the hall of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), causes them to ascend the tower of the five faculties (*indriya*) and enter the chamber of the five powers (*bala*), enables them to smell the fragrance of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and drink the water of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), seats them upon the bed of *sa-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and allows them to touch the cool, untainted breeze of the four dhyānas.
One who is able to do so is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to sentient beings.

Without violating the pure precepts, they are able to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), increase awakened wisdom (*jñāna*), destroy the evil realms, and attain the path of liberation. They contemplate the method of the Four Noble Truths, burn away the weeds of false views, shatter the rock of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and crush the great asuras of attachment to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Clearly seeing the snares of the five desires of Māra, they cross the desolate wilderness and perilous paths to enter the city of Nirvāṇa.

They sever the net of craving, destroy the *piśāca* demons of envy and jealousy, wash away stinginess and greed, and vomit out pride. They humble the notions of "I" and "mine," uproot the three poisons, extinguish all fetters and proclivities, and bring to rest the wheel of birth and death. They cut the cords of attachment to the body and break the chains of causal conditions; they are able to topple the lush, towering trees of the three realms of existence. Thus they forever leave behind the womb, and cross over the great ocean of suffering—old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair.
"If you wish to know the causes and conditions, their essential nature is profound and subtle.
To attempt to explain their true characteristics with limited wisdom is like a person trying to shatter a rocky mountain with their head."
This is the greatest net, encompassing the three realms;
this is the forest of delusion, which confuses practitioners;
this is the evil snare, which ensnares the deer that are ordinary beings.
Those who enter this snare have their wholesome dharmas extinguished; they are like outcaste Mātaṅgas pierced by poisoned arrows.
This is the thicket of wisdom, the thicket that churns the ocean of causes and conditions.
Who has gathered the ocean of conditions? Śākyamuni!
He has perfected great wisdom and the nectar of nirvāṇa.
"These twelve links of dependent origination can only be seen by a Buddha; they enable one to eliminate one's own delusions and to transform others.

As I have heard in the past, King Ceta resided in the city of Ujjayinī. He was diligent in the practice of giving, fond of practicing patience, and respectful toward his elders and seniors. Possessing courageous might and a powerful army, he brought the four seas under his majestic subjugation.
He was skilled in governance and judgment, and in comforting the common people, he was like a mother cow mindful of her calf."
Later, at another time, a great epidemic broke out in the city of Ujjayanī, and those who died exceeded half the population, until the inhabitants of the city became exceedingly few.
Although the people employed incantations and medicines to avert the calamity, it was like pouring clarified butter onto a fire; the affliction increased all the more fierce.
The dead were numerous and the roads were desolate, with few traces of human presence; foxes, wolves, and jackals filled the streets and alleys, even entering the houses of men.
Vultures and eagles flew in flocks, obscuring the sun and moon.
The entire city wailed in grief, and tears flowed in streams upon the roads; the heaps of corpses within the city were like those in a cemetery.

At that time, King Ceta, seeing that many of his subjects had perished, was filled with grief and distress; like one who has entered the ranks of battle and been captured by the enemy, he became emaciated with sorrow and fear, giving rise to such indignation that he forgot the very thought of death.

During the stillness of night, he devised a plan alone and resolved his mind with firm determination. He sought out the pestilence-demon, smeared his entire body with *agada* medicine, bound himself with a consecrated cord, and donned armor of wish-fulfilling jewels. Grasping a sharp sword in his hand, he set out alone, departing from the palace grounds through the main gate. He proceeded to the crossroads of the city, to shrines, temples, and stupas, searching everywhere within wells and beneath bridges, as well as among the trees and market stalls at every location.

He saw various ghosts of diverse appearances and differing voices, cruel and malevolent, killing without restraint. Dead bodies and skeletons were strewn before them; they used skulls as vessels to hold human blood and marrow. With their hands, they groped for entrails and bowels, stained with excrement and blood, or draped human intestines across their bodies, quarreling over the corpses and dragging one another in their struggle to eat.
Thus, malevolent spirits, *chi-mei*, and *wang-liang* filled the city.
Having seen this, the king—like a golden-winged garuḍa wishing to seize a dragon—entered among the ghosts and rebuked them, saying:
"For what reason is this so?"
He asked in verse:
"For what reason do you have human intestines entwined around your body,
holding a skull-bowl in your hand filled to the brim with blood, marrow, and brain?"
“Why are you born as a malignant pestilence, constantly severing the life-root of human beings,
devouring their flesh and blood to satisfy your own hunger?
The ghosts immediately replied with a verse:
“I am a night-roaming demon, who feeds upon the marrow and flesh of humans,
as well as their fat, grease, and five internal organs— all of which I find most delicious.
That you, my subjects, now suffer from this calamity is truly the work of me.”
The king asked again,
"Is it truly you who have committed these calamities?
The rākṣasa replied:
"This was done by me," the king said again to the ghost:
"Why do you not now quickly abandon this matter?"
The spirits replied:
"We cannot abandon it. Why is this? 'The point of a thorn is sharp;
the nature of fire is heat; such is the nature of rākṣasas.'"
"You eat human flesh.
The king said to the ghost,
"Why do you not wish to renounce it now?"
Do you not see that the color of my sword is like a dark blue cloud, like an *utpala* flower, and like a venomous snake when it is in a great rage?
Grasping this sharp blade with the strength of my arm, I am fully capable of making you abandon this evil deed.
The rākṣasa replied:
"O Lord of Men!
You have attained mastery; even if you were to cut my body with a sharp blade until it was like sesame seeds, [I would not be moved]."
"Even though you can do this, the fire of calamity and affliction still cannot be extinguished.
The King asked:
"Why is it not extinguished?"
The rākṣasa immediately pointed toward a great tree and replied to the king:

"Beneath that tree now dwells a great rākṣasa with three eyes on his face, whose gaze flickers restlessly; his appearance is fierce and hideous. By touching with his hands or looking with his eyes, he can bring about calamities and death."
"All diseases are caused by him; he has brought all living beings to their deaths and destruction.
You, Great Being, should first subdue him; if he is humbled, we shall follow suit."
Upon hearing these words, the king ran swiftly toward him and shouted,
"What is your name?
The rākṣasa replied:
“I am named Vehicle-of-the-Belly; I manifest my form according to my will, and by my power, I cause all your people to suffer calamities.
When the king heard this, he cried out:
“Now I have found relief!”
The rākṣasa asked,
"In what sense do you say 'rest'?
The king replied:
"I have long contemplated who among those suffering in the world I might find;
now that I have finally found you, I shall no longer be weary with toil.
The rākṣasa asked:
"What do you intend to do now?
The king said, "This sharp sword of mine has never tasted blood; for the sake of my people, I shall surely drink your blood with this blade as if it were nectar."
The rākṣasa said,
"Though you perform these deeds, they cannot dispel the fruit of your exhaustion.
The king asked:
"What is the fruit of not overcoming weariness?
The rākṣasa replied, "You should now observe that within the southern triple gate there is a rākṣasa named Mahādundubhi; only one who possesses courageous and robust strength can subdue him."
"I shall now remain here and not abandon you to flee; first, you must subdue him.
Upon hearing these words, the king brandished his sword and advanced straight through the great darkness, arriving directly at the southern gate.

He saw the rākṣasa Mahābherī looking up with a haughty gaze, sitting with his legs drawn up; he had three heads upon a body clad in armor, grasping a three-pronged halberd, and was dark blue-black in color, most terrifying to behold.
The king then thought to himself:
"That demon has finished his evil deeds today and enjoys leisure and pleasure, while I alone am miserable and haggard.
By my own majesty and valor, I can cause all other kings to bear me upon their heads; yet I am being tormented by this rākṣasa."
Seeing the king’s majestic and stern authority, the rākṣasa rose in alarm, joined his palms in reverence, placed them upon the crown of his head, and spoke these words:
"Welcome, Great King!"
"His majestic virtue and dignity are like those of Śakra; out of compassion to save the people of the world, he has come to my place.
The king said, "Rākṣasa!"
"You have brought great calamity and suffering upon my subjects; you falsely praise me, yet your deeds are utterly evil.
The rākṣasa said:
"If Your Majesty would trust my words, please listen to what I say: neither the disasters of the world nor its lack of disaster are my doing."

"Outside the city there is a ghost named Mahāśrīṇa, who is the most powerful among those who roam at night; he has four heads and four faces and possesses great majesty. He is my master, and if you can subdue him, you will attain great renown."

Upon hearing these words, the king hurried out of the city. He saw that Rākṣasa wearing a garland of skulls bound upon his four heads, with a moist elephant hide serving as his garment, and further having a python coiled around his waist. Various venomous snakes served as his necklace, and his saw-like fangs protruded from both sides to hang from human bellies. His body was massive and smeared with blood; his hands, feet, and joints were like red sandalwood.

Furthermore, he filled a skull with blood and pus and placed it before him; sighing, inhaling, sipping, and devouring it until he was satiated, he grasped a sharp halberd in his hand and burned the corpses of the dead.

Having seen this, the king’s countenance became stern and his heroic spirit was stirred; like a violent wind blowing against a great tree, or as two lions encounter one another, he immediately displayed his fierce majesty and spoke with a roar: "Ho!..."

"O Lord of the Night, how extreme is your treachery toward me! You have unleashed poisonous evils to harm my people; your incantations and medicinal treatments are like pouring clarified butter onto a fire. Now, the time for your death has arrived!"
The rākṣasa replied:
"Lord of the Earth!
Do not be quick to anger; listen as I first explain the cause of this calamity, and only after questioning me regarding my transgressions should you inflict punishment."
"The calamities and afflictions of the common people are not of my making; yet I am weak and lack autonomy, being driven into service by others.
On this path ahead there is a female demon who drives me on, constraining me so that I have no self-mastery."
The king asked again:
"What was the appearance of that woman? He replied:

"He is extremely evil, feigning kindness and gentleness outwardly while harboring malice and cruelty within his heart; he can momentarily manifest various forms and appearances. You must subdue him, and I shall follow you."
The king then reflected:
"This lack of autonomy must be sought from her.
At that time, the rākṣasī abandoned her own form and transformed herself into the queen whom the king held most dear; walking behind the king, she spoke to him, saying:
"I have always been the one most cherished and esteemed by Your Majesty; why have you abandoned me to travel here at night? Whom else do you now love?
At that moment, the king, having suddenly heard these words, had not yet discerned their truth or falsehood; he turned his head to look back and immediately recognized them to be a ghost.
The king spoke these words to him:
"Venerable One!
Please stay for a moment!"
"You have devoured the inhabitants of an entire city until none remain; yet now you wish to eat me?
It is like a violent river that has the power to sweep away and submerge everything, yet cannot float a massive boulder or a heavy mountain."
The king took her by the hand and said to her:
"Abandon your illusory delusions and restore your original form.
You have committed a great evil; my seizing you now is not unjust."
The rākṣasa immediately joined his palms in salutation and said,
"I now take refuge in the King with a sincere heart.
At that moment, the King again heard a strange sound and looked toward the four quarters.
The rākṣasa asked,
"Why do you look back? The king replied:
"What is this wondrous sound?

The rākṣasa replied, "I was passing by when I heard this singing and the sound of lute-playing; these are my roots. All calamities and afflictions are caused by that woman; it is because of that woman that I am made to dwell here."
At that time, the king immediately realized that this rākṣasī was acting under the command of another; he then seized the singing girl and asked her, "What is your name?
The rākṣasī replied:
"My name is Trivedī. He further said:
"I have yet another king named Caturdaṃṣṭra."
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately dismissed the singing girl and sought out those four-tusked rākṣasas, who were promptly captured.
Then the four-tusked ones said to the king:
"This was not our fault; not far from here there are six rākṣasas:"

The first is named Yunlu (Cloud-Roaring), the second is named Shanye (Mountain-Peak), the third is named Wengfu (Pot-Bellied), the fourth is named Jingangzhu (Vajra-Lord), the fifth is named Jiandu (Poisonous Sight), and the sixth is named Zhijuan (Lasso-Thrower).
"These six rākṣasa youths are my masters.
Upon hearing these words, the king went to their location and immediately captured those six rākṣasas.
The rākṣasa spoke again:
"I, too, am sent by another.
The king then asked:
"Who sent you? The six rākṣasīs replied:
"There are two rākṣasīs:"
"One is named Ox-Ear, and the other is named Hand-Spear.
They can serve me.
The King then had them brought forth.
He spoke again to the king, saying:
"I am not my own master; I have another lord.
The king asked:
"Who is it? The rākṣasa replied,
"His name is the Swift Golden-Winged Bird."
Immediately, he seized that garuḍa again.
The garuḍa said:
"There are three men who are my masters."
The first was named Extremely Evil, the second Fire-Hair, and the third Sandalwood.
The king then reflected:
“I now seek these spirits to extinguish my calamities and afflictions, yet these spirits merely point one another out along a vast road that stretches far and wide.”
"Though it be long and far, if one does not investigate and discover its root, one will never find rest.
The king advanced further and saw three rākṣasīs; seeing the king coming from afar, those rākṣasīs immediately fled.
The king then said: "Wait!
This sharp sword of mine has never yet been used."
"I have come here after traveling a long distance for the sake of protecting my subjects;
why do you abandon me and flee?
Upon hearing the King’s words of consolation, the rākṣasa immediately turned back and, joining his palms, said:

"Not far from here is a vast charnel ground where various wicked birds and beasts have their dens and lairs. Within it, foxes, wolves, jackals, dholes, raccoon dogs, bears, tigers, vultures, eagles, owls, and crows prey upon one another, emitting great and horrific cries that fill the air in every direction."
The king asked again,
"What does he have? They replied:

"There is a rākṣasa there, coarse and large in form, with swollen calves like tumors, laughing, parched, and cracked and peeling from thirst; his color is like a black cloud, his two eyes flicker like flashing lightning, and his sharp fangs protrude doubly as he bites his lip in rage.
He has various spirits as his retinue, and no evil spirits fail to follow him."
All the unrighteousness in the world is their doing; their violent faction is flourishing and is most difficult to subdue.
If you can subdue these powerful spirits, the King’s majesty will spread throughout the world, and we too shall submit and comply.
Upon hearing these words, the king’s valor and resolve surged uncontrollably like the surging waves of the ocean, and he proceeded immediately to that place.
Dust and mist, blinding darkness, fierce winds, and scorching flames blew over the fragments of dead men, shrouding everything in such dense obscurity that nothing could be seen.

He saw that the rākṣasa’s form and appearance were as previously described; surrounding him on all sides, foul odors accumulated in abundance. Everywhere there were heaps of skulls and piles of hair and nails as vast as mountains;
tattered, worn-out clothes were scattered and ruined upon the ground, and broken jars, pots, and shards left no place to walk.
In some places he saw bloated corpses, festering with maggots and decayed; hideous sounds and strange portents filled the air, making it as utterly terrifying as the kalpa of weapons.
Furthermore, there were various ghosts who all subsisted on flesh and blood to nourish themselves with satiety; they were entirely a host of fierce, perilous, and cruel beings.

Their eyes were like flashes of lightning and fire blazed upon their heads; their noses were large, bulbous, and protruding, while two fangs jutted forth. Their ears were shaped like winnowing baskets; their forms were so hideous that they cannot be fully described.
They used the skins of tigers and wolves for their clothing, and placing skulls filled with fat in their right hands, they poured them into the fire.
When the king saw this, he immediately became sorrowful and cried out:
"Alas! What a tragedy!"
"Why do you rely on your own strength and act so violently?
I shall not establish myself unless I first crush and destroy you!
If, by the power of mantras and medicines, the ghosts all flee and disperse, I must now run forward with speed and seize the rākṣasa’s hair with my left hand."
"For the sake of removing calamities and afflictions from my people, I must surely destroy this lord of the rākṣasas.
Having spoken these words, he surveyed the four quarters and immediately leaped up with a roar like that of a lion:
"I take refuge in the various heavens and the deities of the four directions; I shall uproot the poisonous tree that is the root of all calamities within the kingdom."
He immediately stopped his hair.
The rākṣasa, relying on his own strength, laughed mockingly and said:
"Who wishes to cut across this violent river?"
Who would wish to count the teeth in a tiger’s maw?
Who would intentionally come to provoke a fierce and venomous snake?
I have utterly crushed all the heroic and mighty men of the world, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis.
"How dare you suddenly seize my hair?
Leave it be and say no more.

Among all those in the world who possess great power and fierce prowess, there is none at all capable of being my equal, with the sole exception of Cchataka. Who is this petty lad that dares to grasp my hair?"
Upon hearing these words, the king was immediately filled with joy and courage, and he said to the spirit:
"Excellent, worthy sir!
He who spoke the name 'Cchattra' is none other than myself."
Upon hearing these words, the spirit was both startled and delighted, and said:

"Please allow me to repent my transgressions. I pray that Your Majesty will show compassion and refrain from anger; from this day forward, I shall eliminate all calamities and afflictions for Your Majesty."
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.

By the sovereign power of the King, the spirits and deities retreated and dispersed; the people within the kingdom became twice as prosperous and flourishing, free from all calamities and misfortunes, resembling the inhabitants of the heavens.
