Furthermore, for what reason is this parable spoken? It is not for the sake of frivolous speech, nor is it untimely. Why is this so?
In order to expand upon the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma and to reveal the principle of dependent origination, he employs these various and manifold metaphors.
The term "royal city" is a metaphor for the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Within the city of the three realms of existence, there are birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; the suffering of separation from the loved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of encountering the hated; as well as verbal abuse, ill repute, the observance of precepts, and the breaking of precepts—such various and immeasurable sufferings are beyond calculation.

When afflictions and calamities cause the loss of roots of goodness, the Bodhisattva feels compassion for them, like a mother cow mindful of her calf; he acts as a true kinsman to sentient beings, making firm vows with courageous resolve to rescue and deliver all.

They skillfully understand the causes and effects of the fetters and habits of birth and death; they are adept at discerning what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; they are fully endowed with the four means of integration and have accomplished the One Vehicle.

These beings of great resolve observe how those in the five realms of existence revolve in transmigration and suffer, constantly being afflicted by the four great poisonous snakes, the enemy-thieves of the five aggregates, the empty village of the six sense bases, and the deceitful intimacy of craving, as well as by the five desires born of ignorance and the clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self."
"These sentient beings are bound by afflictions; why should I not now deliver them?

Having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva rose from his palace and immediately went forth into homelessness. He donned the armor of diligence, protected himself with the divine spells of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), anointed his body with the excellent medicine of mindfulness of the body, took the merit of patience as his shield, wielded the sharp sword of wisdom cultivated over immeasurable eons, and maintained focused right mindfulness as the king’s great highway.
When sitting at the site of enlightenment, he observed the source of suffering in all worlds and made a great, solemn vow to surely uproot it.

This source of suffering oppresses sentient beings with great anguish; it is the foremost of all afflictions, obscured by the ninety-six kinds of ignorance, such that they do not recognize the origin of the calamities of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, through correct observation, saw the immeasurable suffering and affliction of old age, sickness, and death.
Having understood this meaning, he immediately asked Old Age:
"What is your name?"
The Old Man replied,
"I am named 'Old Age'.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"What is it that you age?
The Old Man replied,
"As for me who ages, I am able to age the three realms."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"What further must be done?
The old man replied:
"I have done nothing.
The Bodhisattva said:
"It was out of craving and attachment that you brought about this famine."
You harbor memories like a wild elephant trampling a plantain grove until it is utterly crushed;
you are a remote and perilous path through the wilderness, capable of extinguishing the pleasures of the six sense faculties;
you can destroy robust physical beauty, like hail destroying flowers and stripping away vigorous vitality.
If one can cause the six sense-faculties to be extinguished and dried up,
how can you say,
"I have done nothing"?
The old man replied,
"This is indeed so.
The Bodhisattva said:
"The two characters 'Lao' (Old) are heard throughout the three realms, yet none understand their true meaning.
Lao spoke again, saying,
"You now truly and exhaustively know me."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Who is that second one?
The old man replied:
"It is called 'Death'.
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately asked Death:
"How can your name be so coarse and evil?"
Death replied:
"It is not merely named 'Evil'; the deeds associated with that name are even more coarse and wicked.
I am capable of killing all beings in every world—humans, devas, asuras, yakṣas, and spirits."
"Just as a great rākṣasa can destroy a kingdom, so too am I able to destroy the lives of all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva asked,
"How strange!"
You are the most wicked of all:
you possess no heart of compassion.
There is nowhere you do not travel; no base and evil karma exceeds yours.
The corpse replied,
"Such a thing is indeed my body.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Though your nature is such, by the power of my mind I shall surely sever you.
Though you are difficult to subdue, by my diligence I shall surely subdue you.
Just as the waves of the ocean cannot blow away a mountain, so it is with you; how could you possibly kill me?"
Mṛtyu replied,
"Though you may now harbor such an intention, I fear you will not necessarily be able to subdue me.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Why do you now doubt that I am incapable?
Death replied,
"If there were one possessed of diligence and skillful means, they would indeed be able to subdue me."
"I fear that you may not necessarily be courageous and diligent; for this reason, I doubt you.
The Bodhisattva said, "You should observe me first, regarding my compassion and skillful means throughout immeasurable kalpas."

I shall offer my own life in exchange for that of all sentient beings; even if a mortal enemy were to sever my limbs and joints with a sharp sword, I would constantly maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward them.
If sentient beings in urgent distress should come to me for refuge, I would rather sacrifice my own body and life to provide them with protection.
"Is this skillful means sufficient to extinguish you, Death?
Death replied, "Why the need for such extensive explanation and repeated exchange? Why trouble me so persistently with such hardship?"
I shall speak to you with utmost sincerity regarding the root; this root is birth itself.

Birth gives rise to all the immeasurable sufferings and afflictions of the world: the four great poisonous snakes, the five aggregates as hostile thieves, the vessel of the six sense-faculties, and the transmigration through the five realms—all these are produced by birth.
In this very life one first encounters all manner of suffering, let alone in the intermediate and subsequent stages;
if one undergoes birth, the suffering such as ours would be beyond measure, but if one abandons birth, there will be no further affliction.
All faults and afflictions arise from birth; for example, without fuel, fire has nothing to burn;
likewise, without a tree, an axe has nothing to chop;
and just as without a jar, what could a mallet break?
If there were no lotus flowers, what would the frost destroy?
Using this as a metaphor, one knows that birth brings many afflictions.
If you now possess sincere resolve and vow to sever death, you must first sever birth.
"Because this arises, there exist old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; all such calamities and misfortunes possess power.
The Bodhisattva said, "I understand this matter: if there were mountains, the vajra would surely destroy them."
If there were no mountain, what could even the diamond be capable of destroying, despite its hardness?
All who possess a body inevitably experience various sufferings; if one has no body, of what could suffering cause one to suffer?
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately released Old Age and Death and seized Birth, asking him:
"What is your name?"
Jāti replied, "I have many various names; as for my name, it is the most excellent among them, and I am called Jāti.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Why is it called 'birth'? Birth replied,
"Observe for yourself."
The Bodhisattva then contemplated birth for himself and spoke these words:
"Indeed, this 'birth' emerges from all existence; the meaning of birth arises from the combination of two syllables."
Jāti replied, "Your wisdom now is truly not a perverted cultivation; you have understood it through correct practice.
The Bodhisattva asked:
“Since this birth gives rise to all suffering, why is it not called ‘the emergence from all suffering,’ but rather simply ‘birth’?
Birth replied, “I do indeed have this fault; it is truly as you say.”
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Do you not see that I possess a firm vow capable of severing yours?
My very essence is compassion, which can extinguish all the sufferings of the world."
Jāti replied: "Excellent, excellent!
It is truly as you have said; I am not independent, for I exist through another who provides me with a basis."
"All men who possess such power are able to give rise to all the sufferings of birth and death.
If you do not believe this, why do you not observe it for yourself?
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"As I now contemplate birth, I know with certainty that it exists.
These three realms of existence (*bhava*) are like three great dragons, capable of raining down torrential showers into the river of birth, which flows into the ocean of death;
they are the river of causal conditions that sweeps sentient beings away, drowning them in the sea of suffering."
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately relinquished birth and grasped existence, rebuking existence, saying:
"I act as a true savior for all sentient beings; wielding the sword of wisdom, I am able to slay my enemies!"
"How is it that you now dare to be so self-indulgent and give rise to such adornment?
One replied immediately:
"The hooks and snares of the four graspings are pulling me along."
"Attached to existence through the four graspings, they powerfully seize the infantile and ignorant. He said:
"I shall provide what can bring pleasure to existence; why do you increase manifold sufferings by providing for existence?"
He took up the response and said:

"For example, just as empty space cannot produce a tree, but a tree can be produced through the causal conditions of earth and water, if there were no water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), by what means could the tree of existence (*bhava*) arise?"
"You should not now merely reproach me!
The Bodhisattva then abandoned the four graspings and seized craving.
Craving spoke to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Welcome, Prince of Śuddhodana!
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, you have performed various meritorious deeds and accumulated all manner of wholesome practices.
Your majestic power surpasses that of Śakra and Mahābrahmā; please deign to accept this humble offering of mine."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"With what will you make an offering? Priya replied:
"The sensual pleasures experienced through the five sense faculties are my offering.
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Why do you offer me these five sense faculties?"
Pramoda replied,
"I invite you with form, fragrance, taste, and touch.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Do you now invite me with fragrant and delicious poisonous fruit?
Tṛṣṇā replied, "Why do you call it poisonous?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"These five desires are like casting a sheep into a fire, or like a blind man falling into a deep pit; they cause one to stray from liberation and close the gate to Nirvana."
"A person of wisdom remains detached from the five desires even in their dreams,
let alone while awake! Ai replied,
"Are not the five desires of the devas superior?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"It is also like an illusion or a dream.

Take, for example, the celestial maiden Sunda, as beautiful as the sun, who rode upon a celestial palace with music at her command; yet when her merit was exhausted and her life ended, she fell back into hell—is this not deception?"
Ānanda replied,
"If you now find fault with the matters of the desire realm, are not the various heavens of the form realm sources of happiness?
Within that form realm, one dwells peacefully in meditative concentration, with few afflictions."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I fully know all the matters of suffering and affliction within that realm of form.
Tṛṣṇā replied:
"How are you now able to observe and know this?
The Bodhisattva replied,
"Though one may attain meditative concentration and be born in the Brahma world, when one's merit is exhausted and life comes to an end, one falls into the three evil realms."
"It is like roasting and broiling someone and then sprinkling them with cold water; sentient beings of meager merit suffer in saṃsāra.
Ai replied, "According to what you understand, even the highest Peak of Existence is, in your mind, as base and contemptible as a blade of grass."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"What is meant by 'the Peak of Existence'? Tṛṣṇā replied:
"The four formless realms are called the 'Summit of Existence' (bhavāgra).
The Bodhisattva asked:
"What are the essential characteristics of the four formless realms?"
Piyadāsa replied,
"Among those gods in the formless realm, there are some whose lifespan is fixed at eighty thousand great kalpas.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"When that great kalpa comes to an end, what further state does one receive? Āyu replied,
"When eighty thousand kalpas have ended, it is called a 'conclusion'."
The Bodhisattva said: "Alas!
How strange!"

One contemplates that the sufferings and afflictions in the desire realm are immeasurable; one observes that the very nature of the form realm must inevitably perish; and even reaching the four formless realms, one cannot escape death.
Within these worlds, joy is scarce while suffering is abundant—how truly pitiable!
Tṛṣṇā replied,
"If you now wish to leave my domain, where else do you intend to seek happiness?
The Bodhisattva asked:
“Where does your realm reside? Tṛṣṇā replied,
“All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are my realm.”
The Bodhisattva said:
"All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are within your domain, wherein death holds mastery.
I have now transcended the realm of the conditioned; death cannot reach me, for I am forever free from the place of death."

It is a place free from the separation from those one loves and the encounter with those one hates; a place without birth, old age, sickness, sorrow, lamentation, or affliction; the place where the five aggregates are exhausted and the five faculties cease; the place where all sense-faculties have no further function; and the place praised by the All-Knowing One as the emergence of the Deathless (Amṛta).
"Is such a place not called 'beyond your domain'?
Having heard this, Tṛṣṇā laughed loudly and said,
"Great seers such as Viśvāmitra and Baka have all spoken these words, yet none of them has ever attained it."
The Bodhisattva said,
"Although he wishes to seek it, he does not know the skillful means.
Prajñākūṭa replied:
"What skillful means do you have now?
The Bodhisattva said:
"You should now abandon the deception of sentient beings and all forms of great arrogance."
"I shall now pull you out, just as a great elephant pulls up a small blade of grass.
Tṛṣṇā replied, "Excellent!"
"O beings of great resolve!
Relying upon sensation, one should first grasp sensation.
The Bodhisattva said:
"I now observe with clear vision that all who are born are universally terrified by the essential nature of suffering.
The sense faculties race about in pursuit of pleasure, yet this pleasure is not self-governed but exists through dependence on others; such pleasure is deceptive and merely a temporary phenomenon."
Ordinary, foolish people, though they repeatedly obtain pleasure, have no sense of satiety;

such pleasure leads to heedlessness, which can plunder the faculties and delude the human mind, causing ordinary beings to fall like flies into honey—where the flavor gained is extremely meager while the loss is immense.
"You do not distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly; as soon as you see something, you give rise to craving. It is like pouring ghee and oil onto a great fire—the flames increase all the more.
Love, wait a moment! Wait until I have captured 'Feeling,' and then I shall deal with you."
"Your offense and mine are exactly equal; we both deserve to be punished.
Tṛṣṇā replied, "O Prince of Śuddhodana!"
Although you are personally determined and wish to harbor this intention, I fear you will not withstand me. Why is this?

In ages past at the beginning of the kalpa, there were great rishis such as Pīṅgala, who appeared during a fortunate time when the lifespan was eighty thousand years; even they, with their profound virtue and conduct, could not diminish my power, let alone you in this degenerate age of the end times, where lifespans are short and do not exceed a hundred years.
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Have I emerged into an evil world?
Tṛṣṇā replied:
"You have truly emerged from an evil age.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Even if today the afflictions are raging and one has emerged during a turbid time, if one does not break through the gate of your ignorance, how can one be called a Great Man?"
Ānanda said: "Stop! Do not praise yourself."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I speak at the proper time and not at an improper time.
This is the right time and the right place; this is speaking what is true, and speaking that which is meaningful."
"Just as the light of the newly risen sun cannot be concealed, the light of wisdom of a Great Man is likewise difficult to obscure.
Māra replied again,
"Observing your resolve, though you advance with courage, I see no sign of success."
"You have repeatedly praised yourself like clouds and thunder heralding the descent of a great rain that brings joy to the peacocks;
yet now you have merely raised the clouds and thunder without seeing any rain fall—what benefit will such drought-thunder provide?"
"I suspect you lack sincerity based on my estimation of your mind.
The Bodhisattva said,
"I shall now demonstrate to you that which is not false."
"The sword of wisdom, honed by the roots of goodness I have accumulated over immeasurable kalpas through single-minded concentration, shall be used to slay you.
Craving replied,
"What is it that ends?"
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"Who now acts as the cause of disturbance for me by producing this song?
Who is it whose hands—bound by the karma and afflictions of the three realms of existence—touch the lute of the triple world, thereby deluding all deceitful and crooked sentient beings?"
Tissa said: "I am merely acting as a guide, just as this singer wishes to play the lute; this is my primary role.
At present, I am acting for his sake and am directed by him."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Is this craving? Craving replied:
"Yes," the Bodhisattva said,
"craving is the greatest fire; it can burn all manner of things and pervades everywhere."
"Those who are attached to pleasure all fall into the midst of craving; the ignorant and foolish fall into it like moths rushing into a flame.
Craving said:
"Observe thoroughly."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I already know this: those who greedily delight in the pleasures of birth and death will surely be harmed by craving;
those birds and beasts that crave flavors will surely be ensnared in nets."
Tṛṣṇā said: "You truly know this.

Nevertheless, I am indeed able to cause all the foolish and ignorant to become attached to worldly pleasures, so that in their future lives they will inevitably be subjected to harsh and rigid suffering."
"The craving of sentient beings for existence and pleasure is what I have created; even those born as high as the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are made to fall back down again.
The Bodhisattva said:
"You do not speak falsely."
"In the world, nothing causes such extreme thirst as craving; it is like drinking salt water, which only increases one's thirst.
Drinking the salt water of existence only increases one's craving. Craving said:
"Do not kill me!
The Bodhisattva said,
"Though your words are good, your mind constantly harbors evil."
"If I do not remove you, how can I find peace?
Although this is so, you must wait a moment while I take [the food] and receive it.
The Bodhisattva reflected:
"From what does sensation arise?

Thus, he exerts himself with vigor of body and mind, free from cowardice; having departed from all clamor and agitation, he attains the foundation of tranquil concentration and enters the ground of omniscience, whereupon he directly perceives sensation.
He spoke to Vedanā, saying:
"For a long time you have deceived and toyed with sentient beings, whereas I act as an uninvited friend to all sentient beings.
From this day forward, you shall no longer be able to cause further disturbances."
The recipient asked,
"What disturbance have I caused?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"The nature of those who possess a body is suffering; they falsely manifest the appearance of happiness to delude the minds of the foolish and ignorant.
Though they appear friendly and kind, they are in truth great enemies.
Thus he replied.
"There is indeed this fault.
Nevertheless, sentient beings still cling to a self, like bees gathering from flowers; they greedily crave their fragrance and flavor, remaining restless and undisturbed.
The Bodhisattva said:
"What you say is true.

Just as people enter the sea for the sake of pleasure and encounter various perils, or enter the ranks of battle for the sake of pleasure and are wounded by one another with arrows falling like rain, and with spears, halberds, swords, and lances."

For the sake of the causes and conditions of pleasure, they travel far along perilous paths through wildernesses, enduring manifold hardships such as hunger and thirst; for the sake of the causes and conditions of pleasure, they perform various ascetic practices: throwing themselves into abysses, leaping into fire, scorching their bodies with the five heats, lying upon beds of thorns, fasting by abstaining from food, sitting on woven rafters, wearing garments of tree bark and grass, and eating only fruits and vegetables.
For the sake of the causes and conditions of pleasure, they construct various implements, plow fields, and cultivate crops;
they build caves and houses, and weave clothing.
Such matters as these, all for the sake of pleasure, give rise to immeasurable suffering.
Vedanā replied:
“It is indeed so.
Yet, for the sake of becoming a cause of happiness for all sentient beings, I am able to undergo immeasurable suffering.”
“I am extremely fickle and restless, never pausing for a moment; yet all sentient beings are attached to the pursuit of pleasure, claiming that I am always present.
The Bodhisattva said:
“All sentient beings are truly to be pitied; from moment to moment they are constantly tormented by thirst for you, and these ignorant and dark beings are disturbed and afflicted by you.”
Feeling replied:
"My faults and afflictions do not end with this alone; there are further transgressions many times greater than these.
Since beginningless time, throughout the realms of existence, I have constantly swallowed and received [the fruits of karma] among all classes of sentient beings, yet I have never known satiety."
"Just as when oil is poured onto a fire, the fire knows no satisfaction; so too do these people delight in and cling to the 'self,' and none among them are able to perceive the faults of this self.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Today, in the presence of this enemy who is my craving, I shall cry out with a loud voice and brandish the sword of wisdom, intending to strike him down."
He spoke with affection, saying:
"This was caused by you; it was not my own fault.
If what he says is indeed true, I shall now execute you.
"If you do not exist, then craving will not exist.
Feeling replied:
"I am not independent; I am driven by contact. Even if you were to harm me, it would bring you no benefit."
The Bodhisattva immediately understood their sequence; with his hand of wisdom, he touched Sparśa and said to him:
"What is your name?"
"The suffering of all sentient beings arises from this.
Because you possess it as a cause, the feet of birth and death increase, and the gate to Nirvana is closed.
Contact said:
"That which can produce feeling is indeed so.

Feeling arises through the causal condition of three things; it is just like drilling for fire: when the human effort, the fire-drill, and the fire-board—these three things—are combined, fire is produced. I am also like this."
When the eye, consciousness, and their object—these three factors—come together, contact arises; with contact as a causal condition, sensation arises.
If the six sense bases did not exist, from what would the "self" arise?
The Bodhisattva said:
"You speak the truth.
Apart from these three causal conditions, there is no contact; the stream that gives rise to contact is most proximate to the six sense faculties."
"Contact, you stay here for now!
I must first apprehend the six sense faculties so that they may share the same guilt as you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having realized the characteristics of contact, proceeded to examine the six sense faculties in turn:

"These six sense faculties are like a swallow's nest or like bubbles on water; they are also like a newly formed boil that will soon burst. What great strength do they possess that you are so arrogant?"
The six sense bases asked,
"Why do you speak these words?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"Because you exist, you exert power over contact; yet, being yourself devoid of any objective reality, you perversely give rise to grasping and produce all suffering.
I have severed all disputes—how could I dispute with you?"
The six sense bases said, "Our transgression is slight; we can only produce contact.
The Bodhisattva said:
"I now observe that contact has its origin in you.

The six sense bases are a vast cavern of immeasurable suffering and affliction; you are constantly wild and unruly, never tranquil in mind, perpetually fickle and never disciplined, and you know no satiety in what you grasp at."
"The six sense organs are infantile and ignorant; they crave and relish the six contacts while seeking after the six sense objects.
The Six Entrances replied:
"O Great-Minded Being!
"If you wish to subdue me, you should first subdue name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
If you strive and toil wishing to obstruct me, you should obstruct name-and-form.
— *The Collection of the Unknowing Rākṣasa*, Middle Volume.
The Collection on the Rākṣasa of Ignorance, Volume Lower (alternatively titled *The Scripture on the Collection on the Rākṣasa of Ignorance*,
translator unknown, appended to the Qin Records).
Once the Bodhisattva had attained the subduing of the six sense bases, he immediately proceeded to contemplate name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Knowing its essential nature and characteristics, he addressed it by the name "Form-and-Matter" (nāmarūpa), saying:
"Because of you as a causal condition, the great suffering of all sentient beings is produced; you should quickly turn back and return to your own karma."
Name-and-Form said,
"I do not see any fault of my own.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Why do you not recognize your own faults now?
You are a deceitful being of extremely evil nature; it is through you as a causal condition that the six sense-faculties of all sentient beings are produced."
Name-and-form replied:
"This is indeed so.
Just as a tree can produce branches and leaves, because there is a self, one is able to produce the branches and leaves of the six sense faculties."
The Bodhisattva said:
"I shall now use the sharp axe of wisdom to cut down your root; the branches and leaves of the six sense-faculties will naturally fall away.
Name-and-Form replied:
“You cannot kill me; it is consciousness—powerful, with strong shoulders and great strength—that constantly protects me.
If this seed of consciousness were not to fall into the ground of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), by what cause could all manner of suffering arise?”
The Bodhisattva said:
"It is truly so.
If consciousness did not dwell within the mother’s womb during the stage of the kalala, the body of a sentient being would never grow or develop."
If consciousness did not abide in the kalala, this kalala would immediately disintegrate; if it were to disintegrate, by what cause could there be the body of a sentient being?
"For this reason, I shall now burn the seed of consciousness with the fire of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva then relinquished name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), observed consciousness (*vijñāna*), and reflected upon it, saying:
"Your nature is deceptive, like a magical illusion; you are as restless and unstable as a monkey, and like a flash of lightning, you never pause for even a moment."
"It is like an unbroken horse that does not stay on the road, or like a mad elephant running wild and difficult to restrain.
Consciousness said,
"Who dares to revile and insult the King of the Conditioned?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Who is it that has made this error by appointing you as king? What marks or characteristics do you possess to claim the title of king?
Consciousness replied:
"I take this body as my city and the six sense bases as its gates.
As I am now truly the lord of this city, with all phenomena following me and taking me as their head, how could I not be the king?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I have whetted the sword of wisdom; now I shall utterly destroy your royal throne.
Consciousness (vijñāna) said:
"How strange! Since I have committed no fault, why do they harbor such resentment and ill will toward me?
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva.
"You speak thus of giving rise to groundless resentment and aversion, yet you yourself give rise to the affliction of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); is this not itself resentment?
Consciousness replied:
"I and name-and-form truly exist in mutual dependence; if there were no consciousness, there would be no name-and-form, and if there were no name-and-form, there would likewise be no consciousness."
The Bodhisattva said:
"How strange!
Name-and-form and consciousness are truly close friends, firmly bound together like glue; they are the very root of the cyclic existence of all sentient beings."
Consciousness replied:
"I am indeed a close and intimate friend to name-and-form;
yet I am driven by karmic formations, placed within karma without autonomy, and according to its goodness or evil, I receive the forms of the five destinies."
The Bodhisattva said:
"You are driven by your own conditioned formations; for such a transgression, I grant you a moment's reprieve.
Although you have committed a fault, wait until my awakening is clear. Now, having observed the formations with the eye of wisdom, I shall then hold you accountable."
The Bodhisattva immediately abandoned consciousness and proceeded to the sphere of formations (*saṃskāra*).
The formations were instantly struck with alarm and said:
"Who are you, who with such valor and strength treats your body as light, donning indestructible armor and grasping in hand the heavy and sharp sword of Bodhi?"
Foolish beings sleep long in the darkness of night, imagining it to be "mine," yet they are able to walk alone within this terrifying, fearsome, and dark abyss of negligence.
The Bodhisattva said:
"The causes and conditions for you receiving this wretched body have been long and far-reaching; today I have investigated and observed them thoroughly, and thus I am named Siddhārtha.
As he spoke, the attendant was startled and said:
“By what means did you attain liberation?
The Bodhisattva replied:
“I made a firm vow in the past to offer worship and respect to the Great Śākyamuni Buddha, bathing him and providing him with food, practicing great diligence until this very day.”
"From that time forward, you have adorned your merit without ever ceasing.
Carya said, "I observe that you have not been adorned for long."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Do not speak such words.
During my first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I had not yet attained certainty; it was only upon completing the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa that I attained certainty, desiring to save sentient beings."
Xing said: "How strange!
Is it possible to love sentient beings?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"I love sentient beings because of compassion; I do not give rise to love through defiled attachment.
Suppose there were a herd of elephants in a great forest and fires broke out on all four sides—who, seeing such calamity, would not feel compassion?"
At that time, the greatest elephant pulled at the branch of a tree to extinguish the fire with its water, guiding the way for them to pass and escape the danger of the flames.
All sentient beings are surrounded by the fires of birth, old age, sickness, and death; what wise person would not give rise to compassion and desire to enable them to emerge from it?
Caryā said: "Since you possess compassion and love for sentient beings, why have you entered into equanimity?
The Bodhisattva replied:
“I have rescued sentient beings without ever having abandoned them!

From the perspective of consciousness, I observe that birth and death, with all their great calamities and afflictions, are your doing; it is for the sake of severing you that I have come to your side.”
Because of you, one is born in the second heaven as Śakra, Lord of Devas, with insatiable desire;
again, because of you, one attains birth in the Brahma-world, sitting upon a lotus throne and entering meditative absorption;
and so on, ascending in succession to the Peak of Existence, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, only to fall into the three evil realms at the end of one's life.
"Such a matter as this was indeed your doing. Xing said, "It is exactly as you have said;
guiding the consciousness toward the royal path was truly my work."
"In the sphere where consciousness operates, I shall protect you and ensure you reach your destination.
The Bodhisattva said:
"With the stone of right view, I shall whet the sword of wisdom and sever your limbs and joints."
Xing said, "Please do not do this!
It will not compensate for the fruit of your exhaustion."
The Bodhisattva asked:
"For what reason do you not mend it?
The practitioner replied:
Ignorance is the spark for all fetters and afflictions, the mother of great suffering.
It is the accumulation of all distress, baseness, and impurity; every calamity and ailment is its creation.
"You do not pursue him, yet you wish instead to seize me;
what benefit will this bring? The Bodhisattva said, "Where is this ignorance located?"
The Practitioner said:
"This ignorance is surrounded by great piśācas and the rākṣasas of affliction, making it difficult to subdue.
It now dwells amidst the various evil graveyards of the fetters and latent tendencies of delusion."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having understood the locus of ignorance through his practice, gave rise to a courageous mind and went to that place, roaring:
"O you rākṣasas of the fetters and you ghosts of affliction!
If I am defeated by them, I shall share in their punishment and execution;
but if I defeat them, I must surely destroy those afflictions, fetters, and evil rākṣasas, so that they are utterly extinguished without remainder!
The Practitioner said:

"Since you possess such courage and steadfast diligence, and have entered the Great Fearless Vajra Samādhi, the gateway of liberation shall open for you of its own accord; what difficulty could there be in utterly extinguishing ignorance?"
At that time, the Bodhisattva, with heroic vigor, looked around in all directions, immediately seized Ignorance, and interrogated him, saying:
"Do you not now dwell within those cemeteries of the various evils of afflictions, habitual tendencies, and karmic fetters?"
Yet this cemetery is a place loathed and despised by those who fear birth and death.

It is a place where the fierce winds of inverted views, worldly dust, and the fetters (saṃyojana) obscure the eye of wisdom so that nothing can be seen; it is a place where various kinds of deceit, crookedness, doubt, and regret gather like heaps of dung and weeds.
Here, the corpses of those who have broken the precepts and the dead from the five desires lie scattered in filth, their limbs rotted and decayed, filling this cemetery.
The great winds of vitarka and vicāra blow upon the fires of the three poisons, their fierce flames blazing intensely;
evil desires and pride stir restlessly, as one laughs aloud amidst a heap of bones;
the corpses of negligence and various unwholesome observances defile the ground with impure pus and blood.
The three realms of existence are like cracked and broken jars, their surfaces fouled and shattered, severing all roots of goodness.

Various broken vessels lie scattered and ruined upon the ground; the hair of eternalism and nihilism is blown about in disarray by the wind; and the tattered rags of shamelessness and lack of remorse are strewn throughout the charnel grounds.

The afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*) are like coarse, harsh stones and sand; the ninety-six kinds of false views are like crows and ravens, while various evil vultures and eagles nest among the burial mounds.
At times there are also sentient beings possessed by craving, such as foxes, wolves, jackals, monkeys, wildcats, and mice, which dwell in holes within the mounds.
Furthermore, there is the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*), like a stumps tree whose branches and leaves have been stripped away, withered and decayed amidst the cemetery.
Furthermore, there is the adjudication of unlawful matters, like a broken bed placed within the cemetery.
At times there are those who throw themselves into deep pools or rush into fires, or lie upon beds of thorns; their various ascetic practices are like a blazing fire consuming a cemetery.
At other times there are those who, relying on their physical strength, as well as their life-span and wealth, are filled with arrogance and impurity, gathering like swarms of flies in a cemetery.
In some cases, there are resentment, enmity, and jealousy—thorns that fill the cemetery.
At other times, there are flies of unwholesome thoughts and reflections that destroy the roots of goodness; and there are impure worms from abscesses, foul and defiling, that gather upon the corpse.

Some are like the five hindrances, afflictions, and hostile thieves dwelling among the burial mounds; others are like sorcerers who calculate "self" and "what belongs to self," gathering together among the burial mounds.
Furthermore, there are various other views and diverse heterodox doctrines, like foxes, owls, and crows uttering great, evil cries and hooting amidst the tombs.

There are also rākṣasas who seize the snares of craving; some rākṣasas hold the mallet of sleep while delighting in the five desires, yet they also grasp trident-forks with three prongs in their hands. They possess all manner of unwholesome and foul complexions, and they run wild with loud shouts, clamoring and laughing forcefully, devoid of any sense of fear.

Some rākṣasas shook their heads and writhed their bodies, glaring with eyes wide with rage as they shrieked; they leaped, bounded, bellowed, and slapped their thighs; some whistled, others sang, and at times they performed dances for sport.

There are the rākṣasīs of anger, the rākṣasīs of harbored resentment, the rākṣasīs of minor evils with heavy retribution, the rākṣasīs of sudden violence, and the rākṣasīs of greed and jealousy; as well as pride, excessive pride, self-pride, inferiority pride, false pride, and great pride; and the desire for what is unlawful, sensual craving, and evil craving—all such fierce and perilous fetters and afflictions, these great rākṣasīs, are beyond counting.

The Bodhisattva went to the cemetery where the heaps of fetters lay; there he beheld the various faults and evils of this ignorance (*avidyā*), which obscures the eye of wisdom and obstructs the source of the body, causing all sentient beings not to see the Four Truths and falling into the evil destinies.

He then spoke these words: "This ignorance acts as the guide on the vast desert road of birth and death; it can ignite the great conflagration of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and is the mother of all afflictions, fetters, and karmic actions."
He closes the gate of *nirvāṇa* and opens the way to the various evil realms. He can assume a massive form that encompasses the three worlds and pervades all places.

His great head is heedlessness; his broad forehead is the knot of doubt; his ugly face is delusive confusion; his nose is a pimple of wrong thoughts; his eyes are false views and the "blind boy"; his flashing lightning-like glances reach the four quarters; he lies in wait for enemies and seeks to repay with evil; his ears are long and pendulous with much hair; he is full of deceit, fraud, and hypocrisy;

his eyebrows are deep, wide, and profound; his sharp fangs are anger and ferocity; his coarse upper lips are the ugliness of greed; his lower lip hangs down, its corners turned back by the corruption of jealousy; and his livelihood is crooked, sycophantic, hollow, and pretentious.

Greed for gain and offerings serves as its sharp teeth; the sixty-two views serve as its hair; the three cravings and voracious appetite serve as its long throat; the eightfold wrong paths and their blemishes serve as its shoulders and arms;

the various unwholesome observances serve as its long claws; the endurance of fetters and karma serves as its two breasts; lack of contentment and bloated arrogance serve as its belly; deep sleep and remorse serve as its navel; much desire and craving serve as its genitals and buttocks; the eighteen elements serve as its two thighs; unlawful desires and evil desires serve as its two knees; and the view of self and the view of a person serve as its feet.

The great elephant of shamelessness wears garments of filthy, damp hides; the elephant of lack of remorse wears a cloak of coarse, foul, and greasy blue wool; he sits upon the bed of the fetters, with the rākṣasas of the various bonds as his attendants.

Regarding those afflictions, the various evil rākṣasas—though one possessed a thousand tongues within this great assembly, even speaking of their transgressions and faults, one could not exhaustively describe them.
Furthermore, one sees the rākṣasa of ignorance, with the seal-wheel of death rotating beside it; when the wise of the world see this, they tremble with dread.
At that time, the Bodhisattva redoubled his diligence and attained a superior state of single-minded concentration.
He experienced great joy and exultation, and immediately thereafter, a sequentially purified mind arose, whereby he attained the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi).
With feet firmly planted, one proceeds to the domain of the rākṣasa of ignorance, reaching the level and even ground of the state free from affliction.
There, one removes all thorns, pebbles, and gravel of the poisonous mind of anger, resentment, and malice.

The eight worldly dharmas are like dust and soil, while the rain of loving-kindness pours down to sprinkle the earth, causing all roots of goodness to grow; these pure, luxuriant, and soft grasses of the roots of goodness bring peace and happiness.
Taking the two feet and the four means of integration as one's foundation, one firmly maintains them, standing out in excellence above the masses.
With the left hand of meditative concentration, he gathers the great tangled hair of the sixty-two views;
with the right hand of wisdom, he draws a sharp sword.
With a mind that does not wait for the request of sentient beings, he lets out a great lion’s roar and proclaims aloud:

“I have accumulated wholesome dharmas under immeasurable Buddhas, vowing to deliver all beings by means of the Great Vehicle; the fruit of my diligence throughout immeasurable eons has now been realized!”

All sentient beings are being scorched by the great fire of birth and death; I should now extinguish it for them, subdue the thieves of the fetters, sever the channels of conditioned formations, and extract them from their perilous difficulties by means of the supramundane path!
When the rākṣasa Ignorance heard this roar, he extended his playful arm and laughed loudly, saying:
"The Great Brahmā King, Maheśvara, Viṣṇu, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the sun, the moon, and the stars—all have knelt before me to be controlled by me."

The seer Vāsava, Vāsuyūpavṛkṣa, Bāli, and other such immeasurable seers, each hoping to escape my realm through their wisdom and virtue, were nonetheless all deluded by me and did not know the path out.
I have placed all sentient beings upon the wheel of birth and death, causing them to transmigrate within the realms of existence without autonomy; such things as these are entirely my doing.
Why does this infant fool, failing to deliberate for himself, seize my hair?
Indeed, all beings—humans, devas, asuras, and others—have been incessantly harassed by my prowess and strength.
"Who are you that have come so swiftly and impetuously to my presence, roaring so loudly before me?
The arousal of your roots of goodness is like the rising of the sun; such a thing as this I have never heard of nor seen before."
All sentient beings are blinded by ignorance; yet you, with the eye of wisdom opened and seeing clearly, examine the subtle and profound to such an extent.
Who, amidst the great waves of the ocean of birth-and-death suffering, can suddenly provide a ferry to enable them to reach the other shore?
All ordinary and foolish beings dwell upon deviant paths; who shall act as their guide to suddenly reveal the true Way?
Who, amidst the great darkness of ignorance, shall suddenly raise the torch of wisdom to illuminate the gloom?
Within the three realms, all accept and obey my teachings and commands; none are able to contravene them.
All the sages and followers of external paths likewise find joy in them. Within my realm, Maheśvara, Mahābrahmā, and the others, through my power, conceive the notion of permanence.
Who is this most supreme person, fearless and possessing such great courage that he does not fear me, daring to seize my hair?
Excellent, excellent!

You must surely have been born from the lineage of the Buddhas; with the power of right contemplation as your incomparable merit and great compassion as your essence, you are certainly a Bodhisattva who pities and rescues sentient beings.
"His virtue is as majestic and sublime as Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains; apart from this superior man, no one in all the world would dare to raise a hand to seize my hair.
The Bodhisattva replied, "What you have said is indeed true and correct."

Since ancient times, all the wholesome deeds I have cultivated have been solely for the sake of rescuing and liberating all sentient beings; as you have described one who is called a "bodhisattva," I am indeed that very person!
Ignorance said: "O Great-minded Being! Your wisdom is unshakable;
you are determined to save others, treating enemies and kin with equal impartiality as if they were of one single flavor, like a blazing, fierce fire that consumes all growing leaves."
"Now you are burning me with the fire of wisdom, and it is just like that.
You are now firm and upright; I shall never dare to disobey your instruction.
The Bodhisattva said:
“I have sealed this place with the marks of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; depart quickly and do not hesitate!

Having spoken these seals, the Rākṣasa of Ignorance, along with the various afflictions and the evil hosts of Mara’s army, fled and took refuge within the ninety-six kinds of heterodox doctrines, dwelling there in a state of delusion.

At that time, the Bodhisattva extensively gathered the various provisions for the factors of enlightenment; without a teacher, he attained solitary awakening and extinguished ignorance. Therefore, all people should cultivate the six perfections and extensively gather wholesome dharmas.
"One who can skillfully contemplate what the Noble Ones have taught will later attain great bliss and understand the profound meaning.
I once heard of a blind man who was playing with a wooden pestle in the midst of empty space;
when the end of the pestle struck the roof and hit a bee hive, the blind man heard the sound of the bees and fled to escape."
In the sky there was a donkey stung by bees; tormented by the venomous pain, it fell down into a deep abyss.
Within the abyss, a wicked dragon harbored fierce resentment; it raised great clouds and thunder, raining down massive hailstones and striking a thunderbolt upon the empty village below.
Within the assembly, malevolent spirits became extremely wrathful and rained down great fires throughout the realm.
Oppressed by these fires, the sentient beings of the world all fled together into the great river.
Devouring the blood, essence, and vital breath of all sentient beings, those who enter the rivers reach that palace;
there they undergo extreme suffering and poison, entering a swirling abyss, and further enter a stone mountain with but a single opening.
Beings emerge from their holes and enter the great ocean; The salt and bitter seawater corrodes their flesh and bones.
They wail and weep loudly, crying out for their parents: "O gods, who among you can rescue and deliver me?"
At that time, there was a divine horse-king on the seashore who constantly fed on naturally ripened grain and rice, remaining robust and spirited.
Hearing the sounds of sentient beings suffering in distress, the horse-king cried out:
"Who now wishes to cross to the other shore and reach Jambudvīpa?"
All those who had fallen into the water raised their right hands and cried out, "Save us! Save us!
The Horse King immediately shook his body, and eighty-four thousand hairs grew forth in dense clusters; those who seized hold of these hairs were all liberated from suffering.

For what reason are these similes cited? The term "blind man" is a metaphor for the ignorance (*avidyā*) of all sentient beings; the "bee" is a metaphor for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); the "donkey" is a metaphor for consciousness (*vijñāna*); the "donkey falling into a pit" is a metaphor for consciousness falling into name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the "empty village" is a metaphor for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the "hail and thunderbolts" are metaphors for the afflictions of impermanence within the six sense bases; the "evil spirits" are a metaphor for contact (*sparśa*); the "rain of fire" is a metaphor for the various sensations (*vedanā*); "throwing oneself into a river" is a metaphor for craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the "rākṣasa in the water devouring the vital essence of humans" is a metaphor for the four graspings (*upādāna*); "entering a whirlpool" is a metaphor for the three realms of existence (*bhava*); the "great stone cavern" is a metaphor for birth (*jāti*); and the "great ocean" is a metaphor for old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and the multitude of sufferings.

The divine horse king is a metaphor for the Buddha, whose body is firm, solid, and robust through virtuous merit and right resolve; who possesses eighty-four thousand hairs of various virtues through right mindfulness and concentration; and who gives rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings.
All sentient beings undergo great suffering; they are born by birth, aged by aging, and died by death.
Yet these sentient beings do not know the skillful means to seek the essential path out of this state, so the Buddhas guide and lead them therein to enable them to escape suffering.

Those capable of riding horses are the practitioners who mount the wheel of Dharma: namely, the five bhikṣus beginning with Kauṇḍinya; the five men beginning with Yaśas; the fifty sons of wealthy and noble elders;

the sixty members of the group from Bhadravarga; the thousand brothers beginning with Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; the two hundred and fifty beginning with Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana; the eighty-four thousand people beginning with King Bimbisāra; and finally Subhadra, down to the eighty-four thousand profound treasuries of the Dharma in the period of the Bequeathed Teaching. If there are sentient beings who hear even a single phrase or a single verse of these, all shall obtain the causal conditions for Great Nirvana.
